name: Newport (Wales)
title: Thickness Gauging in Newport, South Wales | Steel and Bulk Ships
description: Ship thickness measurement in Newport, South Wales, for steel, scrap and bulk carriers and coasters: holds, ballast tanks, hatch covers and piping gauged.
h1: Hull and Tank Gauging for Ships at Newport Docks on the River Usk
intro: Newport's docks open off the River Usk close to where it meets the Severn estuary, and the tide at the river mouth rises and falls by an extraordinary height. Ships lock into the enclosed Alexandra Dock to load steel, scrap and aggregates or to discharge timber, agricultural bulks and project cargo, and while they work there is time to gauge. We send technicians from India for each Newport job; they join the ship at her berth and plan the scope around the cargo sequence and the lock.

highlights.h: A historic sea lock into level water
highlights.p: Newport's South Lock was described as the largest sea lock in the world when it opened shortly before the First World War, and it still admits ships of useful size into a dock where the water stays level. Ships inside lie steadily for days, which suits long tank programmes.

highlights.h: Steel and scrap are hard on holds
highlights.p: Coil, plate and scrap cargoes punish hold structure. Grab damage, dents in tank tops and wastage at hold frame brackets are typical findings, and a ship arriving to load scrap can have each hold gauged while it is still clean and empty.

highlights.h: A tidal river outside the gates
highlights.p: Beyond the dock entrance the Usk runs fast and its banks are left as steep mud slopes at low water. Arrivals and sailings follow the tide closely, so the team boards once the ship is through the lock, and the agent's lock plan decides how long each job really has.

port.h: Newport and the Usk: a deep lock off a tidal river
p: The Port of Newport lies on the west bank of the River Usk just above its mouth on the Severn estuary, a few miles east of Cardiff, and Associated British Ports runs it as part of its South Wales group. The enclosed Alexandra Dock, made up of North and South Docks joined by a passage, is reached from the river through the South Lock, built in the years before the First World War when South Wales coal was shipped around the world. The approach crosses shifting sands in the estuary under pilotage, and the river channel is narrow, so ship movements are scheduled close to high water with tugs in attendance. The Severn's extreme tidal range is felt strongly in the Usk, where the current can run hard on both flood and ebb and the margins dry out to mud for hours either side of low water.

Steel has been at the centre of Newport's trade for generations. The docks handle finished steel and coil linked to the steelworks of South Wales, and scrap metal gathered from across the region is loaded for export to mills overseas. Aggregates and construction materials move in and out, timber and forest products arrive for the building trade, and agricultural bulks, fertiliser and project cargoes make up much of the rest. The ships are typically general cargo and multipurpose ships, handy-sized bulk carriers and coasters, with larger bulk carriers able to use the dock within the limits of the lock. Many are tramp ships fixed voyage by voyage, so a hull seen once may never return, while a few regular trades bring familiar ships back on a predictable cycle that owners can plan inspection around.

Ships usually stay longer at Newport than at a liner port, because bulk loading and discharging by grab takes time and cargo often reaches the quay in batches. A scrap carrier may lie alongside for several days building up a full load, and a ship discharging timber or steel works through her holds in sequence. That rhythm gives the gauging team empty holds and tanks that the crew can ventilate between cargo operations. The dock water stays at one level, so moorings settle and ladders or staging in a hold can be left in place overnight. The main constraint is the river: strong south-westerlies pushing up the estuary in winter, or fog, can delay arrivals and sailings, and a ship that misses her tide waits for the next one, which sometimes leaves the team extra hours on board.

facilities.h: Gauging locations in and around Newport docks
p: The quays of North and South Docks are where almost all of the work is done. Steel and scrap berths have heavy cranes and open storage, and the team works around the stevedores, keeping clear of grab and magnet operations and entering only holds that have been released. Ballast tanks, double bottoms and topside tanks are entered under the ship's permit once the crew has ventilated them and tested the atmosphere. On ships with cranes of their own, the pedestals and jib rests are often added to the scope for magnetic particle checks.

Newport is a bulk and general cargo port rather than a ship-repair centre, so dockings for ships trading here are normally arranged elsewhere in South Wales, on the Mersey or in Cornwall. If a ship lies at a berth outside the dock, she is in fully tidal water, and any work there has to fit the hours when she is afloat and steady. For a superintendent, the sensible pattern is to gauge inside the dock during a cargo call and send the results to the docking yard, which can then plan steel work before the ship arrives rather than after she is on the blocks.
list: North Dock and South Dock quays — hold, tank top and side shell gauging on steel, scrap and bulk ships while cargo is worked.
Scrap loading berths — empty holds measured before the first load goes in, while access is at its easiest.
Lay-by berths in Alexandra Dock — condition surveys on ships waiting for cargo, with time to open tanks in turn.
Project cargo quays — deck, hatch cover and crane pedestal checks on multipurpose ships during heavy lifts.
Ship's cranes and hatch covers — MPI and thickness readings on pedestals, cleats, coamings and jib rests.

context.h: Inspection pressure on tramp ships calling at Newport
p: Port state control at Newport is carried out by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency under the Paris MoU regime, which the UK still follows through its own legislation. Tramp bulk carriers and general cargo ships fixed into scrap and steel trades are often older tonnage, and older ships with a poor inspection record attract more frequent and more detailed inspections. Structural deficiencies in holds, such as wasted frames, holed bulkheads or damaged tank tops, can lead to a detention that loses the charter. Gauging the areas most exposed to grab damage during a quiet day alongside is the straightforward way for an owner to know where the ship stands.

The scrap trade has its own pattern of wear. Heavy, sharp-edged pieces dropped by grab or magnet strike tank tops and lower hopper plating, and residues left in the holds keep moisture against the steel. Charterers fixing ships for scrap may want hold condition documented before loading, and owners need to know whether a ship coming off a scrap voyage needs steel work before her next cargo. The UK rules carried over from the EU ship recycling regulation also expect visiting ships to keep an Inventory of Hazardous Materials on board, which superintendents often review alongside structural condition when deciding how much longer to trade an older ship.

jobs.h: What we gauge for owners at Newport
jobs.p: Newport work is shaped by bulk cargo and by time alongside. Most jobs come from a superintendent who wants condition data before a docking, a charter or a sale, and who knows the ship will spend days in the dock. The team plans holds and tanks around the stevedores' sequence and agrees with the master which spaces can be opened each day. Where a surveyor has asked for particular areas to be checked, those come first, and the rest of the scope follows as access allows. Repeat callers can have a programme split over two visits, while a tramp ship that may not return needs the full scope finished in one stay.
list: Pre-loading hold survey of a bulk carrier fixed for scrap: tank top, hopper and frame gauging before the first grab load.
Third renewal survey preparation on a general cargo ship discharging steel coil, covering double bottom, side shell and hold frames.
Pre-purchase condition gauging of a handy-sized bulk carrier lying in the dock between voyages.
Hatch coaming, cleat and crane pedestal checks with MPI on a multipurpose ship landing project cargo.
Ballast tank and piping gauging on an aggregates coaster, divided across consecutive calls.

logistics: International arrivals are normally through London Heathrow, with onward rail to Newport station on the main line between London and South Wales; Cardiff Airport and Bristol Airport are alternatives for European connections. The team comes from India on UK visas, so we start applications as soon as a Newport call looks likely. The ship's agent books ISPS gate passes for the dock and keeps the team informed of lock times, which govern both boarding and the ship's departure.

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged before a scrap cargo is loaded at Newport?
faqs.a: Yes, and that is the best moment to do it. A bulk carrier usually arrives for scrap with holds swept and empty, so tank top, hopper plating and frames are fully exposed. We gauge them before loading starts, record any grab damage or wastage, and give the owner a dated record of hold condition, which also helps if a damage claim comes up after discharge at the other end.

faqs.q: Does the tide in the Usk limit the work on board?
faqs.a: It limits arrivals and sailings rather than the work itself. The ship enters and leaves through the lock around high water, and inside the dock the level stays constant, so gauging carries on through the tide. We board once the ship is moored inside and aim to finish the essential readings before the outbound lock time the agent gives us.

faqs.q: Where do ships trading to Newport go for drydocking?
faqs.a: Usually to a repair yard elsewhere in South Wales, on the Mersey or in Cornwall, depending on size, availability and the owner's trading pattern. Gauging in the dock at Newport beforehand lets the superintendent send the yard a steel list with quantities, which shortens the docking and cuts down the surprises once the ship is on the blocks.

faqs.q: Can you check cranes and hatch covers for cracks while cargo is worked?
faqs.a: Where the crane or hatch is out of use, yes. Crane pedestals, jib rests, hatch cover cleats and coaming brackets are common places for fatigue cracks on ships that carry heavy steel and scrap. We use magnetic particle inspection on cleaned steel, and dye penetrant where MPI is unsuitable, timed with the chief officer so that the equipment is not needed for cargo while we work.
